J-01.why: The bracket extension pieces arrive as U+0002/U+0003, which are stripped. The math-italic x y z w are then read as code points: 'letter one D four six five'.

J-02.why: Kokoro voices the ⎡⎢⎣ pieces as silence, but the matrix is flattened into 'one zero zero zero one zero zero zero one' with no structure, glued onto the next sentence by the letter-merge rule.

J-03.why: The box-drawing glyphs are silent, but the tree is read as 'app slash renderer slash main dot J S electron slash…', merged into the label and the following sentence. Nothing marks it as code.

J-04.why: Each page number is glued to the start of the next entry ('17 Chapter 2…', '81 J-05'). The dot leaders go to Kokoro as runs of 50+ full stops.

J-05.why: The page number is spoken at the end of the last sentence ('…of a page. two'). The watermark and running header ('SPECIMEN Blitz text test bench Draft 1') are spoken at the start of the next page.

J-06.why: Segmentation is per page, so the sentence is cut at the page break. The first half ends with the page number 'three', and the second half starts with the watermark and running header.

J-07.why: The icon arrives as private-use U+F0E0 and Kokoro voices it as silence. It stays in the string, so the highlight covers it.

J-08.why: Δ arrives as U+0003, and the app strips it to a space: 'the change in momentum, p, over the short interval t'. This reproduces Millington p.60.

J-09.why: Typst drops the zero-width space when it typesets, so it never reaches the PDF. Untested for PDF producers that keep it.

J-10.why: The soft hyphen is invisible and absent from the text layer, so the words read whole.

J-11.why: ❖ and ➤ are silent, but ■ is read 'black square'. Each bullet line becomes its own sentence, which is fine.

J-12.why: The plot labels are read before the caption: 'v (m slash s) t (s)zero A B Figure 1…'. The axis label and the zero weld into '(s)0'.

J-13.why: Kokoro voices the fleurons as silence. There is no extra pause, but nothing wrong is heard.

J-14.why: The gutter line numbers and the code are read inline: 'one two three let total equals zero; for (const x of x s)…'.

J-15.why: The watermark word 'SPECIMEN' is spoken at the top of every J page (see J-05 and J-06). This case's own strings also end with the page number 'four' and the next page's header.

S-01.why: 'delta x', said as one word ('deltax'), but understandable.

S-02.why: All six Greek letters are read by name.

S-03.why: ≤ ≥ ≠ ≈ are all read well, but the sentence-final '3.14.' comes out 'three. fourteen'. Kokoro splits a decimal that ends a sentence.

S-04.why: 'plus or minus', 'times', 'divided by' and 'equals' are all right. 'cm' is read 'see em'.

S-05.why: 'degrees C' rather than 'degrees Celsius', which is acceptable.

S-06.why: % is right, but ‰ is voiced as silence: 'thirty five'.

S-07.why: The currency is read before the amount ('dollar five point nine nine', 'euros twenty', 'rupee one hundred').

S-08.why: pdf.js NFKC turns the micro sign into Greek mu, so 'μm' is 'myoom' and 'μg' is 'myoog'. '9.81 m/s².' becomes 'nine. eighty one em slash es two'.

S-10.why: x² is 'x two'. In 10⁻⁵ the superscript minus and the five are silent: 'ten per second'. H₂O is fine.

S-11.why: Raised digits are flattened: 'x two plus y three', 'ten minus five'. The ordinary PDF case cannot be told apart from 'x2' as a label.

S-12.why: → is 'right arrow' and ↑↓ are 'up arrow' and 'down arrow' (literal, not meaning). ⇒ is silent: 'p q is a premise'.

S-13.why: Every prime is silent: 'f(x) with f(x)', 'five eleven tall'.

S-14.why: 'sum sign', 'integral', 'infinity', 'square root two'. Clumsy but correct.

S-15.why: ∈ ∉ ∀ ∃ and > are all silent: 'for every x S there is a y T; epsilon zero delta zero'.

S-16.why: Math-italic letters are read as code points: 'letter one D four four three (letter one D four three four)'.

S-17.why: ≜ and ⊆ are silent, 𝑓 and 𝑔 are read as code points, and ∝ is right.

S-18.why: § ¶ © ™ ® are all named. The page number 'five' is glued onto the end.

S-19.why: The ellipsis passes through as punctuation. This string also starts with the running header.

S-20.why: The en dash is silent: 'pages ten twenty', 'nineteen ninety nineteen ninety-five', 'London Paris'.

S-21.why: The em dash passes through as punctuation.

S-23.why: 'R and D', 'hash three', 'three:two', 'K M slash H', 'and slash or'. Literal but understandable. The page number is glued on.

P-01.why: NFKC expanded every ligature, and all the words are right.

P-02.why: The line-end hyphen is missed because hasEOL sits on an empty item after the '-'. The result 'trouble- some' is spoken as two words.

P-03.why: The same empty-EOL-item miss: 'well- known self- contained state-of- the-art'. These are audible as small gaps. Where the fix does fire on compound hyphens (real books), it welds them instead (R-12, R-13).

P-04.why: -0.05em is fine. At -0.12em and -0.2em, pdf.js inserts no spaces and the whole line welds into one word.

P-05.why: The letter-spaced heading is spelled out: 'double-u I D E L Y S P A C E D…'.

P-06.why: Small caps extract as mixed case. 'Nasa' and 'Unix' are fine; NASA as an acronym is lost, but it is pronounced correctly anyway.

P-07.why: The drop cap rejoins: 'Once upon a time'.

P-08.why: The footnote markers are read as numbers ('claim one', 'this one two'). The footnote text is read at the foot of the page with its marker glued on ('one the note text…').

P-09.why: Intl.Segmenter splits the URL at '?', making two utterances. The scheme is spelled 'H T T P S colon slash slash'.

P-10.why: 'reader dot help at example dot com'.

P-11.why: 'parse config()', 'foo dot bar(x)', 'get element by I D', 'M A X size'. Fine for prose.

P-12.why: '1e-5' is 'one e five' (the minus is lost). The sentence-final '0.000001' is 'zero. zero zero zero…'. '3.10' is 'three point one zero'.

P-13.why: The ISO date is 'two thousand twenty six dash ten dash twenty four'. The times are 'fourteen:thirty' and 'four:zero five'.

P-14.why: Intl.Segmenter breaks after 'Dr.' and 'et al.', making four utterances and dropping 'Dr.' as a lone 'doctor'. 'e.g.' and 'i.e.' are spelled out.

P-15.why: The quotes and parentheses pass through.

P-16.why: 'one. heat the solution.' The list numbers are read, which is acceptable.

P-18.why: The two columns come out in the right order (Typst emits them in order).

P-19.why: The heading has no full stop, so it runs into the paragraph: 'Energy and Work Work is force times distance'.

P-20.why: 'Chapter roman four', 'Henry roman eight', 'World War roman two'.

P-22.why: The initials split into three one-letter utterances ('J.' 'R.' 'R.'), and 'U.S.A.' is fine.

P-23.why: The bracketed citation numbers are read ('twelve, fourteen'). '[7].' is split off and glued to the next case ID.

P-24.why: The table is flattened row by row, with no structure: 'Element Symbol Mass (u) Hydrogen H one. zero zero eight…'.

P-25.why: The code is read inline ('for (int I equals zero; I N; I plus plus)'). '<' is silent and the page number is glued on.

P-26.why: 'Fe³⁺' is 'fee three' and 'SO₄²⁻' is 'so two'. The charges and subscript four are silent.

M-01.why: Every maths letter is read as a code point: 'letter one D four three eight equals…'.

M-02.why: The stacked fractions flatten to 'a b' and 'one two', and the letters are read as code points.

M-03.why: Code-point letters, then the equation number '(one)'.

M-04.why: 'lim delta letter one D four six one right arrow zero delta…'. The fraction structure is lost.

M-05.why: The matrix is read column by column with code-point thetas.

M-06.why: The sentence of pure maths is read as code points. It merges with the label sentence.

M-07.why: The limits are scrambled ('sum sign n i equals one'), the letters are read as code points, and the next case ID is glued on.

M-08.why: The sub- and superscripts are flattened and read as code points: 'x two i'.

M-09.why: Math-italic Greek is read as code points, and > is silent.

M-10.why: 'square root' survives, but the norm and absolute-value bars are silent and the letters are read as code points.

M-11.why: The combining arrows and hat are silent, ⋅ is silent, and the letters are read as code points.

M-12.why: ∈ is silent, ℝ is read as 'letter two one one D', and > is silent.

M-13.why: The case straddles a page, so the header and page number are inside it. The letters are read as code points.

R-01.why: Every Δ is U+0003 and stripped: 'v equals lim t right arrow zero p t', '( p slash t)'. Nothing tells the listener a symbol is missing.

R-02.why: The bracket pieces are silent, but the vector equation is read flat: 'k a equals k x y z equals k x k y k z'.

R-03.why: The subscript products weld: 'axbx' is read 'aks-buks', 'ayby' is 'eye-bee', 'azbz' is 'az-buz'.

R-04.why: The combining hat is read as 'circumflex' and attached to the previous word ('vectors circumflex a'). cos⁻¹ is 'cos minus one'. The middle dot is silent, and '[2.4]' is 'two point four'.

R-05.why: The running header and page number lead the sentence: 'ten Chapter one Introduction one. four point three THE MATH…'.

R-06.why: The Wingdings bullets arrive as ¾¾ and are read 'three three' (three-quarters glyphs) before every topic.

R-07.why: The scanned page's OCR text layer is letter-split: 'T H E term E R R O R…', 'a M is ta K E'. The text is unrecoverable from spacing.

R-08.why: 'five ten myoog slash D L. roman three.' The range dash is silent, micro becomes mu, and the list numeral 'iii.' is glued on.

R-09.why: The hyphen is missed because hasEOL sits on the empty item. The halves are spoken separately: 'detoxifee kat-eye-un', 'trans ferase', 'peroxi somes'.

R-10.why: The running header with its page number welded on ('one hundred fifty-nine Chapter twelve') leads into the reaction equation, read token by token.

R-11.why: Margin section numbers are read ('two . two . three two . two . four'), and the compound hyphen of tree-walk is dropped: 'treewalk'.

R-12.why: The compound hyphen at the line end is dropped: 'closedover' is read 'klohs-doh-ver'.

R-13.why: 'nineteenthcentury', a compound hyphen dropped. It is still intelligible.

R-14.why: This is the control case. The large numbers, × and ≈ are all read well.

R-15.why: The navigation-bar header is read as a sentence, and the page number ends the paragraph: 'This demonstrates that principled two'.

R-16.why: Code-point letters, ≜ silent, © « ª ® ¬ (mis-mapped bracket pieces) read as 'copyright', 'registered' and 'not sign', and 'dkurt' welded.

R-17.why: The OLS display equation is read inline as a stream of code points.

R-18.why: The nav-bar header, then about 700 characters of equation read as code points. Õ (a mis-mapped ∑) is read 'O tilde'.
